Recall that the distance between vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] in an unweighted undirected graph, [MATH: d(u,v),] is the length (i.e., the number of edges) of the shortest path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v.] If no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, we say that the distance is [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
In a simple undirected unweighted graph [MATH: G=(V,E)] with [MATH: n] vertices [MATH: v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n,] the distance matrix [MATH: D] of the graph is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix (table), where the entry [MATH: a_{ij}] at the intersection of the [MATH: i]th row and the [MATH: j]th column equals the distance between the vertices [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_j.]

Content:
Notice that, according to this definition:

Content:
- If no path exists between [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_j,] then the entry [MATH: a_{ij}] is [MATH: \infty.]
- If [MATH: i=j] (i.e., it is the same vertex), then the entry [MATH: a_{ii}] is [MATH: 0.]
- The distance matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric about the main diagonal.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that the distance between vertices [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] in an unweighted undirected graph, [MATH: d(u,v),] is the length (i.e., the number of edges) of the shortest path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v.] If no path from [MATH: u] to [MATH: v] exists, we say that the distance is [MATH: \infty.]

Content:
In a simple undirected unweighted graph [MATH: G=(V,E)] with [MATH: n] vertices [MATH: v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n,] the distance matrix [MATH: D] of the graph is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix (table), where the entry [MATH: a_{ij}] at the intersection of the [MATH: i]th row and the [MATH: j]th column equals the distance between the vertices [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_j.]

Content:
Notice that, according to this definition:

Content:
- If no path exists between [MATH: v_i] and [MATH: v_j,] then the entry [MATH: a_{ij}] is [MATH: \infty.]
- If [MATH: i=j] (i.e., it is the same vertex), then the entry [MATH: a_{ii}] is [MATH: 0.]
- The distance matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric about the main diagonal.

Content:
Let's look at an example of how to build the distance matrix for the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/573f222dae5b9df7c51804281128625a]

Content:
We start with a square [MATH: 4 \times 4] matrix with [MATH: 0]s on the main diagonal and examine every pair of vertices to determine the remaining matrix entries.

Content:
- The path [MATH: v_2-v_3-v_4] has two edges and is the shortest path between [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_4.] Hence, we write [MATH: 2] in the entry [MATH: a_{24}] and, by symmetry, in the entry [MATH: a_{42}.]

Content:
| | [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: v_2] | [MATH: v_3] | [MATH: v_4] |
| [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: 0] | | | |
| [MATH: v_2] | | [MATH: 0] | | [MATH: 2] |
| [MATH: v_3] | | | [MATH: 0] | |
| [MATH: v_4] | | [MATH: 2] | | [MATH: 0] |

Content:
- Since the vertices [MATH: v_2] and [MATH: v_3] are adjacent, the shortest path between them is [MATH: 1.] Hence, we write [MATH: 1] in the entry [MATH: a_{23}] and, by symmetry, in the entry [MATH: a_{32}.] Similarly, since [MATH: v_3] and [MATH: v_4] are adjacent, we write [MATH: 1] in the entry [MATH: a_{34}] and [MATH: a_{43}.]

Content:
| | [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: v_2] | [MATH: v_3] | [MATH: v_4] |
| [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: 0] | | | |
| [MATH: v_2] | | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] |
| [MATH: v_3] | | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: v_4] | | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] |

- Since the vertex [MATH: v_1] is isolated, the distance from it to any other vertex is [MATH: \infty.] Hence, we write [MATH: \infty] in every entry of the [MATH: 1]st row and in every entry of the [MATH: 1]st column, except for [MATH: a_{11}.]

Content:
| | [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: v_2] | [MATH: v_3] | [MATH: v_4] |
| [MATH: v_1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: \infty] | [MATH: \infty] | [MATH: \infty] |
